reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails
clinicalPearls: Habit-tic deformity is a self-induced nail change produced by repetitive picking or rubbing of the proximal nail fold, most often of the thumb
It classically shows a central longitudinal depression crossed by many parallel transverse ridges, giving a washboard or fir-tree appearance
An enlarged lunula and damage to the cuticle of the affected nail are common accompanying signs
The habit is frequently subconscious, and patients may not connect the repeated manipulation with the nail change
It is distinguished from median canaliform dystrophy, which shows a central split or canal rather than a picked-fold pattern, although the two overlap
Diagnosis is clinical, based on the pattern and a history of manipulation, and no biopsy is usually needed
Management focuses on behavioural awareness and physically protecting the nail fold, for example with occlusive tape or a barrier, to allow normal growth
reference.pathophysiology: Habit-tic deformity results from chronic mechanical trauma inflicted by the patient on their own proximal nail fold and cuticle, typically by picking or rubbing with an adjacent finger. The repeated injury to the region overlying the matrix produces a series of transverse depressions in the plate as it is laid down, arranged around a central longitudinal groove, so that the nail acquires a rippled, washboard surface. Because the damage is to the soft tissue over the matrix rather than the matrix being intrinsically diseased, the nail can recover fully once the manipulation stops, and the enlarged lunula reflects the ongoing disturbance of the proximal nail unit.
additionalDifferentials: Beau lines from systemic matrix arrest
Nail changes of chronic eczema of the fingertip
Onychotillomania and other self-induced nail disorders
Myxoid cyst causing a longitudinal groove
additionalInvestigations: History specifically exploring picking, rubbing, or other repetitive nail manipulation
Clinical inspection for the central groove, transverse ridges, and enlarged lunula
Examination of the cuticle and proximal nail fold for chronic damage
Onychoscopy to characterise the ridging pattern
Assessment for underlying anxiety or a body-focused repetitive behaviour
Photographic monitoring to confirm improvement once manipulation ceases
redFlags: Severe or extensive self-injury suggesting an underlying psychological disorder needing support
Signs of secondary infection of the traumatised nail fold
Features atypical for habit-tic that raise concern for a tumour causing a groove
Failure to improve despite cessation of manipulation, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The deformity is benign and reversible, and the nail grows out normally once the repetitive trauma stops, although relapse is common if the underlying habit persists and behavioural change can be difficult to sustain.
pitfalls: Failing to elicit the self-manipulation history and mislabelling the change as intrinsic nail disease
Confusing it with median canaliform dystrophy and applying the wrong management
Overlooking an associated body-focused repetitive behaviour or anxiety disorder
Expecting improvement without addressing the causative habit
references: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
management: Stop the repetitive picking or rubbing of the proximal nail fold, as behavioural cessation is the definitive treatment that allows the nail to regrow normally
Use physical barrier measures such as occlusive tape or an adhesive dressing over the nail fold, or a fixed nail cover, to interrupt the habit
Offer habit-reversal behavioural therapy and treat any underlying anxiety or body-focused repetitive behaviour
Restore the damaged cuticle and proximal nail fold with emollients and cuticle care
Consider a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor or N-acetylcysteine for an associated body-focused repetitive behaviour when behavioural measures fail
Use photographic monitoring to demonstrate improvement and reinforce cessation, referring to psychology or psychiatry if the habit is entrenched
